It is the wrong tool for mixed-source truth where 3200K rooms meet 5600K windows as a relationship: that is Tungsten Balance , a white-balance fact, not only a honey LUT. Golden Hour is actual low sun, a capture window you can grade warm, not a synonym.
how: Bias the grade toward 2800K to 4000K in the mids. Let practicals and candles carry the key when you can ( Candlelight , Practical Lighting ).
Keep whites from clipping to paper unless overexposure is the point. Skin should look blooded, not jaundiced; pull green if tungsten goes sick.
Prompt: Warm amber grade on [Subject], tungsten honey, candle and practical glow, safety or nostalgia in the mids.
when: Use it for home, memory, or invitation: a kitchen at night, a hotel corridor that wants you. Do not use it as sepia, and do not honey a crime scene that should stay merciless.
vs: Sepia is a brown-gold toned scale, not full color. Golden Hour is a time of day.
Tungsten Balance is the camera's white balance at about 3200K, which can make windows blue. Teal and Orange warms skin while cooling the world.
Candlelight is the source; warm-amber is the overall grade.
examples_film: Amélie keeps interiors in inviting warm practical color so Paris is a hearth. The Grand Budapest Hotel paints hotel spaces with designed warm (and pastel) invitation.
Grammar of hospitality in the mids, not a copied lobby.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Sepia or Teal and Orange . The tell is no true hue left, or cyan streets with only the face warm.
Fix: overall amber bias, lamps as hearths, color still present in costumes and walls.

faq.q: What is warm amber in film?
faq.a: It is an overall warm grade: tungsten honey, candle, and practical glow in the midtones. The world reads as inviting, domestic, or remembered, with hues still present.

faq.q: Warm Amber vs Sepia
faq.a: Warm amber is a color image biased toward honey. Sepia is a brown-gold tone replacing the grey scale, with modern chroma mostly gone. One is hospitality. The other is a print of the past.

faq.q: When should I use warm amber?
faq.a: Use it for home, memory, or invitation. Skip it for merciless worlds, toned-print flashbacks, and complementary teal-orange nights.

faq.q: How do I prompt warm amber for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Warm amber grade on [Subject], tungsten honey, candle and practical glow, safety or nostalgia in the mids. Forbid sepia toning and teal complementary walls.

title: Architexture
narrative: When the set is the subject, human plot becomes a visitor. Concrete, glass, carpet, and window bands do the talking.
A figure gives scale, then disappears into the pattern. It is the wrong tool when a close-up of a lie is the scene.
Architecture cannot deliver an eye twitch. If you drown a dialogue in facade, you will photograph a building and call it a conversation.
This is not automatically one-point ceremony. A flat elevation, a brutalist soffit, a repeating office ceiling can be architexture without a vanishing tunnel.
how: Expose for the material: raking light for relief, or flat light for graphic grids. Use a longer lens to compress floors into texture, or a wide lens close to a wall so the body is tiny against a single plane.

Stop down so brick and joint stay sharp if texture is the point. Prompt: Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.
when: Use it when place outweighs person: first arrival in a city, a worker in a machine, a critic of a monument. Do not use it as the only coverage of an intimate scene.
vs: One-Point Perspective aims space as a tunnel. Architexture may be a flat, tactile wall.
Repetition and Pattern counts units. Architexture can be irregular material, poured and stained.
Extreme Long Shot shrinks a person in land. This shrinks them in built matter.
Windows makes apertures the subject. Architexture may have almost no people in those apertures.
examples_film: Playtime ( PlayTime ) lets modern Paris eat its visitors: glass, grid, and waiting room as comedy of texture. The Brutalist language puts poured mass and material ahead of comfort.
The person remains, as scale. Grammar of buildings, not a tourist postcard.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a human portrait with a famous building behind. The tell is a large face and a postcard sliver of facade.
The fix is to step back or go longer until the body is a module among modules, or to admit you wanted a portrait and drop the claim.

faq.q: What is architexture in film?
faq.a: It is composition that treats architecture as the subject: facades, grids, and materials filling the frame. A person remains as a detail or a scale figure. The set owns space.

faq.q: Architexture vs One-Point Perspective
faq.a: One-point perspective is a tunnel of receding parallels, often ceremonial. Architexture is material and module, which might be a flat wall, a ceiling grid, or a poured mass with no vanishing showpiece. They can combine in a designed hall. They need not.

faq.q: When should I use architexture?
faq.a: Use it when the building is the story: arrival, labor, monument, a system of rooms. Do not use it as the only shot of a face that must be read.

faq.q: How do I prompt architexture for AI image or video?
faq.a: Make the person small in material. Example: Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building. Name concrete, glass, or grid. Forbid portrait crop.

title: Asymmetry
narrative: Who owns space is unsettled. A woman in a corridor may occupy a sliver while red wallpaper and a lamp own the rest.
A driver may sit in a third of night while neon and road own the surplus. The counterweight is the point, not the empty accident of a bad mark.
It is the wrong tool when the scene is a ceremony of order. If both sides should salute, shoot the mirror.
If the character should be presented as an altar, do not hide them in a wing. Asymmetry is not automatically thirds.
Thirds is one recipe for offset. You can hang a figure in a far corner and balance them with a bright speck, which is visual weight, not a student grid.
how: Place the main body off the centerline. Find a counterweight: a practical, a second figure, a block of color, a window.
Check the frame on a monitor without overlay first. If it tips over, add weight or crop.
A slightly wide lens (32mm to 40mm) lets the unused field stay a real place. Prompt: Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror.
when: Use it for desire, class, loneliness, and any conversation where the room is not fair. Do not use it as a default mess: unmotivated clutter is not balance.
vs: Rule of Thirds is a specific offset grid. Asymmetry is the larger family.
Visual Weight is the currency that makes an unequal picture hold. Symmetry is the opposite claim.
Short Siding is a harsh asymmetric trap that denies look-space rather than composing a counterweight. Negative Space lets emptiness itself be the other mass.
examples_film: In the Mood for Love parks bodies in corridors and door gaps so wallpaper, lamps, and rain own as much as faces. Drive lets night, steel, and neon outweigh a still driver.
The pictures hold because something answers the offset. Grammar, not mood boards.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a failed centered shot. The tell is a person who missed their mark and nothing answering them.
The fix is to add a real counterweight, move them to a thirds intersection, or recenter and own Symmetry .

faq.q: What is asymmetry in film?
faq.a: It is a composition that does not mirror. The main mass sits off-axis and is answered by a different mass: light, color, a small figure, empty weather. The frame holds by tension, not by reflection.

faq.q: Asymmetry vs Rule of Thirds
faq.a: Thirds is one offset recipe: lines at one-third. Asymmetry includes thirds and also stranger diagrams, a body in a corner balanced by a bright speck or a void. If you only know thirds, every offset will look like homework.

faq.q: When should I use asymmetry?
faq.a: Use it when the room is not fair: desire, class, isolation, a look that cannot have a mirror. Do not use it as leftover clutter. If nothing answers the offset, the picture just tips.

faq.q: How do I prompt asymmetry for AI image or video?
faq.a: State the offset and the counterweight. Example: Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror. Name the side and the answering object. Avoid the word messy unless mess is the counterweight.

title: Centered Composition
narrative: Control, ritual, comedy, and fate all like this diagram. The person does not borrow space from a third.
The room reports to them, or pretends to. Who owns space is settled in advance by the architecture.

It is the wrong tool for eavesdropping, pursuit, and most dialogue that needs a look-off. If the sides are busy with unequal life, you have an offset picture with a centered head, which is a different sentence.
Wes Anderson made the grammar famous, which is a reason to be precise. Formality is the instrument.
Pastel luggage is not.
how: Square the camera to the back wall. Match left and right masses, or let a planned mismatch be the only joke.
Keep the lens on the centerline of the set, not a casual handheld approximation. A 27mm to 40mm will show the room's obedience.

Longer glass will crop the salute and leave you with mere central framing. Prompt: Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar.
when: Use it for a ritual entrance, a desk of power, a dollhouse comedy, or a fate that feels designed. Do not use it on a chase or a whispered aside that should feel stolen.
vs: Central Framing only demands the body on the crosshairs. Centered composition demands the field.
Symmetry is the stronger claim that left mirrors right. You can center a subject in a room that is not a mirror.
One-Point Perspective adds a vanishing point on the same axis, a tunnel instead of a flat altar. Tableau holds the arrangement in time.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel builds hotel interiors as frontal altars. Moonrise Kingdom presents tents, churches, and children as arranged diagrams.
Both films let a small human deviation read loudly because the axis was so clean. Grammar, not a production-design costume.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a centered head in an uncomposed room. The tell is a bullseye face with a plant on one side and a door on the other.
The fix is to square the camera, match the masses, or switch to Central Framing and let the mess be honest.

faq.q: What is centered composition in film?
faq.a: The dominant subject sits on the central axis, and the rest of the picture is organized around that axis. The frame becomes a frontal tableau. The person is an altar. Leftover space does not belong to a look-off.

faq.q: Centered Composition vs Symmetry
faq.a: Centered composition puts the subject on the axis. Symmetry mirrors masses across that axis. A centered desk in a lopsided office is centered without being symmetrical. A mirrored hall with nobody in the middle is symmetrical without a centered hero.

faq.q: When should I use centered composition?
faq.a: Use it for control, ritual, comedy, or fate: someone presented by a room that obeys. Do not use it when the character should be hunting through space or hiding in someone else's diagram.

faq.q: How do I prompt centered composition for AI image or video?
faq.a: Demand the axis and the room. Example: Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar. Say camera square to the back wall. If you only say centered face, you will get a portrait crop.

title: Central Framing
narrative: Put them on the crosshairs and the diagram changes. Off-center space no longer belongs to the look.
Both leftover fields become equal attendants. The subject owns the axis.
Everyone else owns the wings. It is the wrong tool when the character should be hunting, fleeing, or eavesdropping.
A center punch on a spy in a crowd makes them a poster. A center punch on a god, a child in costume, a dictator, or a comic stiff makes the formality legible.
You can center-punch a face in a messy room. That is still central framing.
The architecture does not have to salute. If the whole room salutes, you have walked into centered composition and maybe into symmetry.
how: Align the lens axis with the sternum or the bridge of the nose. Keep verticals upright unless you want a joke or a threat.
A longer lens (65mm to 85mm) isolates the bullseye. A wider lens will show whether the room is also axial.
Check both ears have similar leftover, then decide if that equality is the point. Prompt: Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame.
when: Use it when a character must be presented, judged, or worshipped: an arrival through doors, a formal portrait, a comic stare into lens. Do not use it on a look-off that needs air in front of the eyes.
vs: Centered Composition organizes the entire field around the axis, often as a frontal tableau. Central framing can be just the body on the crosshairs.
Symmetry mirrors masses. You can punch a face dead center in an asymmetric street.
Rule of Thirds is the default you are breaking. One-Point Perspective adds a vanishing point on that same axis.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel center-punches concierges and guests as if they were stamps. Moonrise Kingdom does the same with children in uniform, frontal and unembarrassed.
The formality is the joke and the tenderness. Grammar, not a Wes Anderson costume kit.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is thirds with a slightly lazy offset. The tell is more air on the look side than behind the head.
The fix is to slide the figure until both leftover fields match, or to admit you wanted Lead Room and keep the offset.

faq.q: What is central framing in film?
faq.a: It is dead-center placement of the figure on the optical axis, a center punch. The body sits on the crosshairs. Leftover space on both sides is equal. The person is presented, not nested into a third.

faq.q: Central Framing vs Centered Composition
faq.a: Central framing is where the body sits: on the axis. Centered composition is the whole diagram: furniture, walls, and other bodies often join the altar. You can center-punch a face in a messy room. That is central framing without a full centered tableau.

faq.q: When should I use central framing?
faq.a: Use it to present, judge, or joke: a formal arrival, a portrait, a child in a uniform, a tyrant at a desk. Do not use it when the look needs air, or when the character should feel like a guest in someone else's frame.

faq.q: How do I prompt central framing for AI image or video?
faq.a: Say dead center and optical axis. Example: Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame. Add square to camera. If you only write portrait, you will get thirds.

title: Clean Frame
narrative: Nothing extra. Who owns space is whoever you left in the rectangle.
A driver against night, a bottle on seamless, a dancer in a cleared hall: the edges do not argue. It is the wrong tool for eavesdropping and for documentary crowding.
, a clean frame may be a lie unless someone in the story has already tidied for an inspection. Clean is not the same as empty.
A fully dressed set can still be clean if no lamp, plant, or shoulder nicks the four sides. Negative space is extra emptiness.
Clean is extra discipline.
how: Clear the near field. Watch all four edges on the monitor.
Use flags and art department, not only a long lens. A longer lens helps by excluding, but a wide clean frame is a stronger claim: you composed the whole room and still kept the borders empty.
Stop down if you need the empty walls sharp. Prompt: Clean frame of [Subject], edges empty, no accidental objects, studio-poster clarity, isolation by tidiness.
when: Use it for product, ritual, poster portraits, and any character who lives in control. Do not clean a view that should feel stolen.
vs: Dirty Frame occupies the edges. That is the opposite ethic.

Negative Space makes emptiness a mass, which a clean frame may also do, but a clean frame can be full of designed set as long as the borders are tidy. Centered Composition often wants clean edges so the altar is not nibbled.
Void deletes the world. Clean still allows a world, just a disciplined one.
examples_film: Drive isolates night figures and cars with poster discipline: edges held, little accident. Product cinema clears tables until an object is a monument.
The grammar is control. A scuff on that control should be intended.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a dirty street pretending to be a poster, or a Void you got by turning off the lights. The tell is a stray shoulder, a plant in the corner, or a black field with no place.
The fix is to clear the edges or to admit you wanted occupied edges and shoot Dirty Frame .

faq.q: What is a clean frame in film?
faq.a: The edges are empty of accidental objects. Every inch is chosen. Isolation comes from tidiness. The camera is granted a view, not a peephole.

faq.q: Clean Frame vs Negative Space
faq.a: Negative space is a large empty mass that acts in the story. A clean frame is about edges without accident. You can have a crowded, designed interior that is still clean at the borders. You can also have dirty edges around a tiny figure in a huge sky.

faq.q: When should I use a clean frame?
faq.a: Use it for control, product, ritual, and poster isolation. Do not tidy a stolen view or a documentary crush.

faq.q: How do I prompt clean frame for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ban occluders. Example: Clean frame of [Subject], edges empty, no accidental objects, studio-poster clarity, isolation by tidiness. Add no foreground objects at the edges. Models love plants in corners. Forbid them.

title: Tonal Contrast
narrative: Make a poster out of a frame and the eye cannot miss the subject. A white face in a black room, a black coat on a white street, a lighthouse beam cutting tar: value owns space more loudly than furniture.
It is the wrong tool for a scene that lives in complexion, food, or mixed daylight conversation. If you crush the mids, you lose the sweat.
Not every picture should be a woodcut. Tonal contrast is composition, not automatically Low-Key Lighting lighting.
You can shoot high contrast at noon with hard sun and deep shade. Low-key is a lighting ratio.
Contrast composition is where the masses sit.
how: Meter for the winner. Let the other mass fall off or blow, on purpose.
Hard light and a dark flag help. A backlight rim can keep a dark figure readable on dark.
Expose for highlights if the subject is the bright mass. Kill fill if the subject is the dark mass on a bright field.
Prompt: High tonal contrast composition with [Subject] as the lightest or darkest mass, graphic punch, no mid-gray mush.
when: Use it for night hunts, moral binaries, graphic titles, and any beat that should read at a distance. Do not crush a scene whose information lives in the midtones.
vs: Low-Key Lighting is a lighting style with dominant shadow. Tonal contrast can also be a bright graphic (white wall, black figure).
Silhouette gives up interior detail. Contrast composition may still keep an eye.
Figure-Ground is the broader first-read split, including color and focus. Chiaroscuro is the painterly modeling of form with light and dark, which may be less poster-flat.
Void deletes the field. Contrast still has two masses.
examples_film: Sin City language turns faces and streets into ink and paper. The Lighthouse grinds value until salt, beam, and body are almost woodcut.
Both make composition out of value first. Grammar, not a comic-panel kit to steal.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is muddy mid-grey. The tell is a face, a wall, and a coat all sitting in the same value band.
The fix is to pick the lightest or darkest mass and send the rest away with flags, exposure, or costume.

faq.q: What is tonal contrast in film?
faq.a: It is a composition built from strong light and dark masses, with the subject as one of those poles. The picture reads as a graphic. Mid-grey detail is reduced so value, not clutter, owns the frame.

faq.q: Tonal Contrast vs Low-Key Lighting
faq.a: Low-key is a lighting ratio: little fill, dominant shadow. Tonal contrast is where light and dark sit as shapes. A noon street with hard sun and deep shade can be high contrast without being a night interior. A low-key room can still be a soft, detailed face.

faq.q: When should I use tonal contrast?
faq.a: Use it when the shot should read as a poster: night, moral split, graphic title, a figure as a cut-out. Do not crush scenes that need skin, food, or mixed conversation detail.

faq.q: How do I prompt tonal contrast for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the poles. Example: High tonal contrast composition with [Subject] as the lightest or darkest mass, graphic punch, no mid-gray mush. Say which one they are. Ban even illumination.

title: Diagonal Composition
narrative: Stillness would be a lie if the scene is a riot, a chase down stairs, or a city that will not sit square. Diagonals shove the eye and refuse a calm horizon of furniture.

It is the wrong tool for a formal treaty, a joke about order, or a face that needs to be an altar. If you roll the camera to fake a diagonal that the set does not have, you have made a dutch angle, which is a different sentence.
A single strong bias line can be enough: a banister, a shadow, a gun. Filling the frame with accidental slants is not composition.
It is a crooked set.
how: Keep the head level unless you truly want a dutch. Find a bias vector in blocking or architecture and place the subject on it or against it.
A wider lens increases the thrust of a receding diagonal. Hard light can throw a diagonal shadow as a second line.
Prompt: Diagonal composition through [Subject], energy on the bias, unstable, rain or stairs as the line.
when: Use it for stairs, street corners, rain, battles, and any beat where a level diagram would calm the scene down. Do not roll the camera to counterfeit a line the location does not offer.
vs: Dutch Angle rolls the camera so the horizon itself tilts. Diagonal composition can keep a true horizon while stairs and bodies cut across.
Leading Lines may be diagonal, but they can also be straight corridors on axis. One-Point Perspective is usually a square, ceremonial tunnel.
Asymmetry offsets mass without requiring a bias line.
examples_film: Battleship Potemkin drives rifles, stairs, and crowds on the bias so the massacre cannot sit still. The Third Man turns Vienna's streets, stairs, and wet shadows into diagonal traps while the camera is often simply in the right place.
Grammar of instability, not a tilt preset.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dutch Angle . The tell is a tilted horizon and no architectural diagonal.
The fix is to level the camera and find stairs, a corner, or a gesture that actually cuts the frame.

faq.q: What is diagonal composition in film?
faq.a: It is a picture organized on the bias: stairs, streets, rain, bodies, shadows as diagonal vectors. Energy and instability come from those lines. The camera may remain level. The set does the tilting.

faq.q: Diagonal Composition vs Dutch Angle
faq.a: A dutch angle rolls the camera so the whole world lists. Diagonal composition uses lines already in the scene. You can have both, but a rolled horizon is not automatically a diagonal composition, and stairs on a level camera are not a dutch.

faq.q: When should I use diagonal composition?
faq.a: Use it when a square, restful diagram would lie: pursuit, stairs, street violence, weather that cuts. Do not use it as a default slant on a calm interior.

faq.q: How do I prompt diagonal composition for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the bias and whether the camera is level. Example: Diagonal composition through [Subject], energy on the bias, unstable, rain or stairs as the line. Specify the line. Add horizon level to block an unwanted dutch.

title: Dirty Frame
narrative: Dirty versus clean edges is a moral diagram. Clean edges say the picture was granted.
Dirty edges say it was stolen, crowded, or survived. A shoulder in the foreground, a plant slicing a corner, rain on a window: someone else owns the near space.
It is the wrong tool for a product, a formal portrait, or a ritual altar. If the edges are dirty because the set was not cleared, you have clutter, not voyeur layers.
A dirty frame can still be composed. The chew should be intentional shapes, not a boom or a coffee cup.
how: Put matter close to the four edges or to the ones that should feel occupied. Open the aperture so that matter melts, unless a sharp shoulder is the eavesdropper.
A longer lens compresses crowd into the edges. A wider lens needs objects truly near the glass.
Check that faces still clear a hole in the middle. Prompt: Dirty frame around [Subject], out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chewing the edges, voyeur layers.
when: Use it for surveillance, parties, streets, and any view that should feel unauthorized or crowded. Do not dirty a ceremonial single or a product hold.
vs: Foreground Interest is a salient near object that may sit in one region. Dirty frame is specifically about edges being occupied, often all around.
Frame within Frame cuts a hard inner rectangle. Dirty matter is usually soft and irregular.
Voyeur is the concealment position that often produces dirty edges. Clean Frame is the opposite ethic: empty edges, isolation by tidiness.
Layered Depth may keep those edge layers sharp if they carry action.
examples_film: The Conversation watches through crowds, glass, and occupied space so privacy is already compromised. Children of Men keeps debris, bodies, and near matter in the aperture so the future never grants a poster.
Grammar of occupancy, not a blur sticker.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is accidental clutter, or a Clean Frame with a fake vignette. The tell is a boom, a logo, or a blurry oval that is not an object.
The fix is to choose the occluders, place them on the edges, and open the lens so they melt without covering the mouth.

faq.q: What is a dirty frame in film?
faq.a: Out-of-focus or near matter chews the edges: shoulders, glass, foliage, crowd. The view is occupied. The camera feels inside a space we were not invited to stand in, or inside a crowd that will not clear.

faq.q: Dirty Frame vs Clean Frame
faq.a: A dirty frame occupies the edges. A clean frame keeps them empty of accident. One isolates by obstruction and complicity. The other isolates by tidiness. Choose the ethic. Do not mix them by forgetting to clear a table.

faq.q: When should I use a dirty frame?
faq.a: Use it when the view should feel stolen, crowded, or physically situated: surveillance, parties, streets, affairs. Do not use it on a formal altar or a product.

faq.q: How do I prompt dirty frame for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the occluders and the edges. Example: Dirty frame around [Subject], out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chewing the edges, voyeur layers. Models default to clean margins. You must demand occupied edges.

title: Figure-Ground
narrative: First read is survival. A face against a matching wall disappears.
A dark coat against a dark street disappears. The audience should not have to hunt the subject unless hunting is the beat (camouflage, a sniper, a ghost).
It is the wrong tool to solve with a fake halo on every shot. Sometimes the story is that they do not separate: a clerk eaten by an office, a dancer eaten by a crowd.
Then you are composing fusion on purpose. Clean edges help.
Dirty edges and busy wallpaper fight figure-ground unless the figure has a stronger currency: backlight rim, color, or a pool of focus.
how: Park the subject against a simpler or opposite field. A rim or backlight traces the outline.
A shallow plane of focus melts the ground. A costume change (dark on light, light on dark, a single saturated piece) is cheaper than a new set.

Check a squint test: if the silhouette dies when you defocus your eyes, the split is weak. Prompt: Clear figure-ground separation of [Subject] from background, contrast of tone, color, or focus so the person reads instantly.
when: Use it as default whenever a person must be found immediately: coverage, posters, any beat that is not hide-and-seek. Do not separate a character who is meant to be eaten by the room.
vs: Silhouette is a hard version: figure as outline against a brighter field, interior detail sacrificed. Shallow Focus buys separation with optics.
Figure-ground can also be a sharp, deep picture with tonal contrast. Tonal Contrast is the graphic extreme of lightest versus darkest mass.
Cameo Lighting isolates with a pool against dark. Architexture may intentionally lose the person in the building.
examples_film: Classical cinematography treats instant separation as manners: rim, backlight, and costume contrast so a face reads in a theater. Westerns park figures against sky.
Noir parks them against wet highlights. When a film withholds the split, it is usually a hide, not a mistake.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a matching suit on a matching wall. The tell is a hunt for the head.
The fix is a rim, a different backdrop value, a costume change, or Shallow Focus . If they should vanish, own it and stop claiming a portrait.

faq.q: What is figure-ground in film?
faq.a: It is the split between the subject and the field so the figure reads immediately. Tone, color, or focus can do the job. If the person and the wall share a value, the composition has not separated them.

faq.q: Figure-Ground vs Silhouette
faq.a: A silhouette is figure-ground taken to outline: the field is brighter, the interior of the body goes dark. Figure-ground also includes a fully lit face against a darker or softer field. Silhouette sacrifices face for shape. Figure-ground may keep the face.

faq.q: When should I use figure-ground?
faq.a: By default, whenever the audience must find the person in a glance. Withhold it when camouflage, crowd, or architecture should swallow them.

faq.q: How do I prompt figure-ground for AI image or video?
faq.a: State how they separate. Example: Clear figure-ground separation of [Subject] from background, contrast of tone, color, or focus so the person reads instantly. Add dark coat against snow, or shallow focus, or rim light. Models often blend subject and wallpaper.

title: Foreground Interest
narrative: The diagram now has a landlord in front of the camera. A bedpost, a shoulder, a glass of whisky can own the near third while the scene happens beyond.
We feel physically situated. Sometimes we feel we should not be there.
It is the wrong tool when the near object covers the decisive face or when it is random clutter. A plant in focus in front of an important mouth is not depth.
It is a mistake. Foreground interest can be sharp (a gun on a table, Kane's objects) or soft (flowers as a veil).
Sharp near matter stages power. Soft near matter stages eavesdropping.
how: Place a real object close to the lens, on a plane that reads as obstacle. Coordinate its edge with eyes and hands so it conceals by design.
A wide or moderate wide (24mm to 40mm) exaggerates the near mass. Open the aperture if the layer should melt.
Stop down if the near object is information. Prompt: Strong foreground object between lens and [Subject], dirty aperture of flowers, fence, or glass, layered depth.
when: Use it to put the camera in a room that already has stuff, to spy, or to show a power object in front of a distant person. Do not let the foreground eat the expression you came for.
vs: Dirty Frame specifically chews the outer edges, often all around, as voyeur layers. Foreground interest can be a designed object in the lower frame without dirty corners.
Layered Depth asks midground and background to carry action too, not just a pretty veil. Frame within Frame uses a hard inner rectangle rather than an object.
Voyeur is the concealment ethic that often uses this layer.
examples_film: Citizen Kane loads tables and objects in the near plane while deals happen beyond. The Graduate frames Benjamin through Mrs.
Robinson's bent leg, a joke of obstruction and power. In the Mood for Love watches through walls and gaps.
The Revenant uses brush, breath, and near nature as obstacles, not stickers.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is accidental clutter. The tell is a menu board or a head slicing a mouth with no relationship to the beat.
The fix is to choose the object, place its edge, and pick focus on purpose. Random foreground is not occluded observation.

faq.q: What is foreground interest in film?
faq.a: A near object sits between lens and subject and does a job: depth, scale, entry, or concealment. Flowers, fence, glass, a table, a body. The camera is in a place, not on a seamless studio axis.

faq.q: Foreground Interest vs Dirty Frame
faq.a: Foreground interest is a salient near layer, which may sit in one region of the picture. A dirty frame occupies the edges, often around the whole aperture, with out-of-focus matter. A whisky glass on a table can be foreground interest in a otherwise clean frame.

faq.q: When should I use foreground interest?
faq.a: Use it when we should feel situated, blocked, or complicit: eavesdropping, a power object in front of a deal, nature in front of a figure. Do not cover the decisive expression by accident.

faq.q: How do I prompt foreground interest for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the object and the focus. Example: Strong foreground object between lens and [Subject], dirty aperture of flowers, fence, or glass, layered depth. Replace the object with the actual thing. State whether that layer is sharp or soft.

title: Frame within Frame
narrative: Someone is watched, trapped, or pictured. The inner frame decides who is allowed in the picture of the picture.
A man in a doorway is either coming home or locked out, depending on which side of the jamb we stand. It is the wrong tool when the second rectangle is only a pretty arch behind a centered face.
If nobody could enter or leave that aperture, you added a sticker. Dirty edges chew.
A frame-in-frame cuts a clean inner border. You can have both: a dirty outer view through a clean door.
Decide which border owns the subject.
how: Compose two rectangles. Place the camera so the inner opening has readable sides, top, and (often) threshold.
Control exposure between the two spaces: interior warm, exterior cold, or the reverse. A moderate wide (32mm to 40mm) shows both borders.
If the inner frame swallows the outer, you have simply recropped. Prompt: Frame-within-frame around [Subject], doorway, window, mirror, or arch as a second rectangle, nested attention.
when: Use it for arrivals, farewells, affairs in corridors, and anyone pictured by a house. Do not drop a random arch behind a portrait and call it nested attention.
vs: Dirty Frame occupies the outer edges with out-of-focus matter. Frame-in-frame is a graphic inner border, often sharp.
Windows stacks many apertures until the building is a grid of shots. Screen in Screen is a picture that is itself a display.
Negative Space can surround a small inner frame with emptiness. Voyeur is the ethical position of watching through that aperture from concealment.
examples_film: The Searchers opens and closes on doorway compositions: desert and home as two countries split by a jamb. In the Mood for Love uses doorframes and corridor gaps to contain encounters that cannot be public.
Entering or leaving the inner rectangle is the cut you do not have to make.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a decorative arch. The tell is an ornamental curve that nobody could walk through, with the subject already filling the screen.
The fix is to show the inner border on at least three sides and to give the threshold a job.

faq.q: What is frame within frame in film?
faq.a: An architectural or graphic border inside the screen encloses the subject: door, window, arch, mirror, gap. There are two rectangles. The inner one decides belonging, exclusion, or being pictured.

faq.q: Frame within Frame vs Dirty Frame
faq.a: A dirty frame chews the outer edges with shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd, often soft. A frame within a frame is a second hard rectangle around the action. One is occupancy of the edge. The other is a nested border. They can combine.

faq.q: When should I use frame within frame?
faq.a: Use it when someone is watched, trapped, welcomed, or pictured by a building. A crossing of the threshold should be able to matter. Do not use it as a pretty inner crop on a portrait.

faq.q: How do I prompt frame within frame for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for a second rectangle and name it. Example: Frame-within-frame around [Subject], doorway, window, mirror, or arch as a second rectangle, nested attention. State which side of the threshold we occupy and the exposure split.

title: Golden Ratio
narrative: Phi is a more secret order than thirds. The diagram still asks who owns space, but the large field is not a blunt two-thirds slab.

A spiral from a corner through a face, then through a doorway, then into empty weather, can feel inevitable without announcing a grid. It is the wrong tool when the audience needs the diagram in one glance.
Action geography, comedy blocking, and most coverage live on simpler axes. If you cannot point to a curve the eye actually rides, you are decorating with math.
Painters used these proportions because canvases hold still. In a moving shot the spiral has to survive a pan, a walk, and a focus change.
Design the still first, then see if the move keeps the curve.
how: A phi grid places lines at about 38 percent and 62 percent, inward of a thirds overlay. A golden spiral is a path, not a stamp: start at a quiet corner and coil toward the face or the object of the look.
Keep the camera level. Moderate glass (40mm to 65mm) preserves the proportions.
Ultra-wide will fake a spiral by bending the room. Prompt: Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid.
when: Use it on a painterly hold: a portrait in a designed room, a landscape where a path, a tree, and a figure actually coil. Do not overlay a spiral on a shot whose masses do not sit on that curve.
vs: Rule of Thirds is the coarser default, lines at one-third, faster to set. Centered Composition plants the subject on the axis and ignores the spiral.
Leading Lines can trace the same curve if the architecture supplies it, but leading lines do not require phi. If the picture is a bullseye, you wanted Central Framing .
examples_film: Painterly cinema often organizes near these proportions without announcing them. Barry Lyndon holds figures and furniture in quiet harmonic rooms.
The Tree of Life lets landscape, light, and a small body share a coil rather than a grid. Portrait of a Lady on Fire stages faces and firelight as a slow curve of attention.
Grammar, not overlays to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is thirds with a spiral graphic imagined on top. The tell is a face on a 33 percent line and a prompt that only says golden.
The fix is to move the mass inward toward 62 percent, or to build an actual path of secondary objects the eye can ride.

faq.q: What is golden ratio in film?
faq.a: It is composition that uses proportions near 1.618, as a phi grid or as a spiral path through the masses. The subject is offset, but not as bluntly as on a thirds line. The eye is meant to travel, not to park on a cell.

faq.q: Golden Ratio vs Rule of Thirds
faq.a: Thirds splits the frame at 33 percent. Phi splits nearer 38 and 62 percent. Thirds is a default grid on a monitor. Golden-ratio composition is a tighter proportional claim, sometimes a curve. Both beat accidental centering. Neither is a law.

faq.q: When should I use golden ratio?
faq.a: Use it when a still or a slow hold has a real path of masses, and you want order that does not look like a student overlay. Skip it for fast geography, jokes, and any shot where the spiral would be a lie.

faq.q: How do I prompt golden ratio for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for a spiral or phi placement and name the path. Example: Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid. State the start of the coil and the landing point. Avoid mystic math talk.

title: Headroom
narrative: The vertical diagram is easy to ignore until it is wrong. Too much accidental headroom makes a person sink, a student error.
Too little clips thought. Deliberate surplus (a nun under a pale wall, a man under oil derricks) makes emptiness a partner.
It is the wrong tool to 'fix' by always parking the eyes on a thirds line. Some faces need to be crushed under a ceiling.
Some need to float. The rule of thirds is a default for the eyes, not a law for the top edge.
Headroom talks to costume and architecture. A tall hat, a halo lamp, a beam: the top edge is a character.
how: Measure from hair to the frame line, not from eyes. For a standard close-up, leave a modest band, enough that a nod will not clip.
For pressure, shave it to a hair. For weather or faith, drop the face in the lower third and let ceiling or sky own the rest.
Tilt and pedestal change headroom without changing lens. Prompt: Deliberate headroom on [Subject], either tight to the hair (pressure) or generously open (air, God, sky).
when: Use tight headroom when the room is a trap or the thought has no ceiling. Use open headroom when land, church, or sky must outweigh the skull.
Do not leave extra sky because you failed to tilt down.
vs: Lead Room is horizontal air in the direction of motion. Headroom is vertical.
Close-Up is a size that makes headroom mistakes loud. Negative Space often lives in surplus headroom.
Short Siding crushes the look horizontally. Void can eat everything above a face until there is no ceiling, only nothing.
examples_film: Classical coverage keeps modest headroom so a nod survives. Ida uses large upper fields of wall and sky as designed surplus, faces low in the diagram.
There Will Be Blood lets derricks and air dwarf a skull. Grammar of the top edge, not a crop preset.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is accidental sink, a figure dropped because the operator did not tilt. The tell is leftover ceiling with no job and eyes nowhere near a decision.
The fix is to tilt down for a standard portrait, or to own the surplus as Negative Space and compose the face low on purpose.

faq.q: What is headroom in film?
faq.a: It is the gap between the top of the head and the top of the frame. Small gap: pressure. Large gap: air, architecture, or weather owns the upper field. Accidental large gap is a common error. Deliberate large gap is a composition.

faq.q: Headroom vs Lead Room
faq.a: Headroom is vertical space above the skull. Lead room is horizontal space in the direction of a walk or a look. You can have generous lead room and tight headroom in the same single. They are different edges of the diagram.

faq.q: When should I use headroom?
faq.a: Always, as a decision. Tighten it to press. Open it when sky or ceiling should act. Do not leave extra air because you missed the tilt.

faq.q: How do I prompt headroom for AI image or video?
faq.a: Say tight or generous and name the upper field. Example: Deliberate headroom on [Subject], either tight to the hair (pressure) or generously open (air, God, sky). Models default to too much sky. Be explicit.

title: Layered Depth
narrative: Social geometry becomes visible at once. Adults sign a boy's future in a near room while the boy plays in a distant window.
A phone booth and a piano split a bar. Who owns space is a matter of which plane can still act.
It is the wrong tool when only one plane has story. Three pretty layers of wallpaper are not layered depth.
If you cannot imagine walking from the near object to the far door, the diagram is a collage. Do not assume every deep stage must be uniformly sharp.
You can hold two actions and still rack. The arrangement is the composition.
The iris is the optics.
how: Place meaningful bodies or objects on separate planes with readable gaps. Keep sightlines and entrances clear.
Choose a wider lens and more distance if you want natural deep space. Stop down (and add light) if several planes must be sharp.
A split diopter is a different cheat. Prompt: Three-plane composition around [Subject], foreground, mid, and deep background all carrying information, deep staging.
when: Use it when two relationships must be true in one hold: a deal and a child, a dance and a call, a guard and a prisoner. Do not stack bric-a-brac in three zones and call it staging.
vs: Deep Focus is the optical result of small aperture and sufficient light, or a digital imitation. Layered depth can exist with selective focus.
Foreground Interest only guarantees a near layer. Layered depth requires the far planes to work.
Tableau may be deep or flat, but it privileges a fixed arrangement over cutting. One-Point Perspective can organize the walkable space as a tunnel.
examples_film: Citizen Kane stages Kane's future indoors while the boy plays outside the window, planes in one sentence. The Best Years of Our Lives splits a bar between piano and telephone booth so attention has to choose.
The Conformist uses fascist architecture as deep, walkable politics. Grammar of staging, not a focus preset.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Deep Focus wallpaper. The tell is everything sharp and only one action.
The fix is to put a second story on another plane, or to admit you wanted a single-plane portrait and simplify.

faq.q: What is layered depth in film?
faq.a: Important actions occupy different distances in one composition. Foreground, midground, and background can all carry information. The shot is walkable. That arrangement is depth staging, whether or not every plane is sharp.

faq.q: Layered Depth vs Deep Focus
faq.a: Layered depth is spatial organization: who stands where. Deep focus is optics: how much is sharp. You can stage three planes and rack between them. You can also stop down so the whole stage holds. Do not conflate the two.

faq.q: When should I use layered depth?
faq.a: Use it when two or more relationships should be visible at once without a cut. Skip it when only one plane has a job. Pretty receding walls are not enough.

faq.q: How do I prompt layered depth for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name three planes and their actions. Example: Three-plane composition around [Subject], foreground, mid, and deep background all carrying information, deep staging. State focus treatment. If you only say depth, you may get blur and no staging.

title: Lead Room
narrative: The horizontal diagram assigns the future. Air in front of the nose is the path, the other person, the door.
Air behind the skull is the past or a trap. Classical coverage buys this air by default.
It is the wrong tool when the character has nowhere to go. A prisoner, a liar pinned by a question, a car about to hit a wall: giving them lead room is politeness the scene does not want.
Lead room is not automatically thirds. You can give a walker a huge field (almost a landscape) or a modest band in a close-up.
The direction of the surplus is the definition.
how: Put the look or the motion toward the empty side. If they walk screen-left, leave more frame on the left.
Pan with a walker to keep that surplus, or let them eat it if arrival is the point. A profile needs more lead than a three-quarter.
Prompt: Lead room in front of [Subject]'s look or walk, more space in the direction of attention than behind, forward narrative.
when: Use it for walks, looks that will be answered, and any coverage that should feel like forward grammar. Do not give lead room to a character you mean to trap.
That is Short Siding 's job.
vs: Short Siding crushes the look against the edge they face and parks dead air behind them. Rule of Thirds often creates lead room as a side effect of an offset face.
Look Space is the field a gaze owns, especially when the object is off-screen. Lead room includes motion.
A still look can be either, but a sprint is lead room first. Headroom is the vertical cousin.
examples_film: Classical coverage puts looking room in front of singles as default grammar, from studio talkies onward. Westerns and road films extend that air into landscape so a rider has a country to enter.
When a film withholds it, you feel the withheld future immediately.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Short Siding by accident. The tell is a profile kissing the edge they look toward, with a warehouse of wallpaper behind the hair.
The fix is to pan toward the look until the surplus sits ahead, unless the trap was intended.

faq.q: What is lead room in film?
faq.a: It is extra space in the direction of a look or a move. More frame ahead of the nose than behind the head. The surplus is the path. Classical coverage treats it as default manners.

faq.q: Lead Room vs Short Siding
faq.a: Lead room gives the character air to look or walk into. Short siding puts the face against the edge it faces and leaves the empty field behind. One is forward grammar. The other is a trap or a jolt.

faq.q: When should I use lead room?
faq.a: Use it when they are going somewhere, even standing: a look that will cut to an object, a walk, a car in motion. Do not use it when you mean to deny the future.

faq.q: How do I prompt lead room for AI image or video?
faq.a: State the look direction and the surplus. Example: Lead room in front of [Subject]'s look or walk, more space in the direction of attention than behind, forward narrative. Say looking screen-left, empty frame ahead of the eyes.

title: Leading Lines
narrative: If a corridor, a rail, or a carpet chevron aims at a person, that person owns the destination and the building owns the path. If the lines aim past them, the person is a gate and infinity owns the rest.
It is the wrong tool when the location has no honest vector. Drawing implied arrows in a bland room is a graphic lie.
A close-up that needs only a face does not need a railroad. Lines can be one-point, two-point, or even a curve.
The job is the same: decide where the eye is forced to land, and whether that landing is a face, a door, or a vanishing field.
how: Find real edges in the set: baseboards, rails, a road, a shadow from a hard source. Place the camera so those edges converge on the intended mass.
A wider lens (24mm to 35mm) strengthens convergence. A long lens flattens lines into stacks, which is compression, not pointing.
Keep the horizon level unless the line itself is a dutch. Prompt: Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure.
when: Use it when a location can aim: station, hotel hall, highway, trench, church nave. Do not invent converging furniture in a set that is actually a box of leftovers.
vs: Vanishing Point is where parallel lines appear to meet. Leading lines may never meet in frame.
One-Point Perspective is a full axial construction with one dominant vanishing point. Leading lines can be a single railing cutting a messy room.
Diagonal Composition uses bias energy even when nothing converges. Architexture fills the frame with material until pointing is secondary.
examples_film: The Shining aims carpets, halls, and a tricycle path at whatever waits. The Deer Hunter uses steel, roads, and industrial edges to shove attention through working space.
The lines are geography, not stickers. Grammar, not a maze to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a centered portrait with random architecture. The tell is a face in the middle and walls that do not aim.
The fix is to move the camera until an edge actually hits the subject, or to drop the claim and shoot a clean portrait.

faq.q: What is leading lines in film?
faq.a: They are real edges in the picture (rails, roads, corridors, shadows, gestures) that steer the eye toward a mass or through the frame. The architecture points. The landing is a choice: face, door, or empty distance.

faq.q: Leading Lines vs One-Point Perspective
faq.a: One-point perspective is a camera squared to a plane with a single vanishing point, often on axis. Leading lines are any vectors that aim. A diagonal railing in a messy street can lead without being a Kubrick hall.

faq.q: When should I use leading lines?
faq.a: Use them when the set can honestly point: a hall, a track, a road, a nave. Skip them in a close-up that only needs a face, and skip them in a room with no true edge toward the subject.

faq.q: How do I prompt leading lines for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the lines and the target. Example: Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure. Specify material. If the lines should continue past the person, say so.

title: Look Space
narrative: A face and a rectangle of unused air can be a whole scene. We wait for the object: a person entering, a painting, a courtyard window.
The subject does not own the surplus. The unseen does.
It is the wrong tool when there is no look. Empty space beside a face that stares into lens is not look-space.
It is leftover. If you need the object on-screen, put it there and stop pretending the air is a mystery.
Look-space is the composition. The POV cut is the completion.
You can hold the look and never pay off, which is a different cruelty.
how: Place more frame in the gaze direction than behind the head, unless you are short-siding. Match the height and direction of the look if the next shot is the object.
A profile or three-quarter makes the owned field obvious. Do not fill that field with competing faces unless the competition is the point.
Prompt: Generous look space for [Subject], the off-screen gaze owning a field of air, tension in what we cannot see.
when: Use it when the object of attention is off-screen or about to enter: a watcher, a painter, a sniper, a lover at a door. Do not leave dead air beside a to-camera interview and call it a look.
vs: Lead Room includes motion and classical manners for a walk. Look-space is specifically the gaze, especially toward an off-screen object.
Point of View is the shot of what they see. Look-space is the shot of them seeing.
Short Siding withholds this field. Reaction Shot may be a look with almost no space if the face is the whole event.
Frame within Frame can put the object in a window inside the look-space.
examples_film: Rear Window builds Jeff's looks and then pays them with courtyard activity. Portrait of a Lady on Fire makes looking the subject, space between painter and model as the true field.
The Stendhal Syndrome matches Anna's looks to museum paintings. Grammar of eyeline, not a tourist view to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is leftover wallpaper, or a false eyeline cut. The tell is empty space on the wrong side of the face, or a next shot the look could not geometrically reach.
The fix is to put the surplus in the gaze direction and to match height and angle if you complete the look.

faq.q: What is look space in film?
faq.a: It is the area of frame a gaze owns, usually ahead of the eyes. Often the important object is off-screen, so the air is tension. In editing, the look may be joined to a shot of what is seen.

faq.q: Look Space vs Lead Room
faq.a: Lead room is space in the direction of movement, and by extension a standing look. Look space is the gaze as a relationship to an object, present or withheld. A runner needs lead room. A watcher of a courtyard needs look-space. They overlap in a still profile. They are not the same job.

faq.q: When should I use look space?
faq.a: Use it when what matters is off-screen or about to arrive, and the face watching is the present tense. Do not confuse leftover margin on an interview with a look.

faq.q: How do I prompt look space for AI image or video?
faq.a: Point the eyes and empty the field they face. Example: Generous look space for [Subject], the off-screen gaze owning a field of air, tension in what we cannot see. Say the object is not in frame. For video, you can add a second shot as POV.

title: Negative Space
narrative: Loneliness needs room. So does dread, and so does waiting.

A face low under a slab of architecture, a man tiny in a desert, a woman with a blank wall as her partner: the empty area is the other character. It is the wrong tool when the scene is crowded with story.
If the blank wall is just an unlit set, you underexposed a failure. Empty is not automatically meaningful.

Unbalanced framing and short-sided composition are cousins, not synonyms. Negative space can sit above a head (headroom as weather), beside a look (air as future), or all around a speck (the world as indifference).
how: Decide what the unoccupied area means before you widen. Control eyeline, headroom, and background detail.
A longer lens can isolate a small figure against a simple field. A wide lens can make the field truly large.
Do not automatically rebalance. Stop down if the empty weather must stay a texture, or open up if it should melt to tone.
Prompt: Vast negative space around [Subject], the figure small, absence as weight, Antonioni emptiness.
when: Use it when isolation, waiting, or land must outweigh a person: a figure under sky, a face under ceiling, a body at the edge of a pale wall. Do not confuse a blank backdrop with a designed void, and do not auto-balance if the imbalance is the beat.
vs: Extreme Long Shot is a size that often produces this space. Negative space can also crush a close face under ceiling.
Short Siding specifically denies look-space. Negative space may sit in any direction.
Void erases the set into nothing. Negative space still belongs to a world.
Clean Frame tidies edges without requiring a small subject. Headroom is the vertical slice of this idea.
examples_film: Ida parks faces low under large fields of architecture and sky. L'Avventura lets islands and empty coasts outweigh the searchers.
Her uses pale interiors and city air as partners for a small body. Mr.
Turner subordinates figures to weather. No Country for Old Men lets landscape refuse comfort.
Grammar of absence, not a desert kit.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Long Shot with a busy horizon. The tell is a small figure against cluttered detail that competes.
The fix is to simplify the field, or to own the clutter as Architexture instead of claiming emptiness.

faq.q: What is negative space in film?
faq.a: It is a large unoccupied area around or beside the subject that still reads as world: sky, wall, snow, sea. The empty field has weight. The person does not automatically own the frame.

faq.q: Negative Space vs Void
faq.a: Negative space is emptiness inside a place. Void erases the place: a figure against black, white, or nothing. Ida's sky is negative space. A body in an unlit nowhere is a void. Both isolate. Only one still has geography.

faq.q: When should I use negative space?
faq.a: Use it when absence should act: isolation, waiting, land that does not care. Do not use it as an unlit wall you forgot to dress. Tie the imbalance to pressure in the scene.

faq.q: How do I prompt negative space for AI image or video?
faq.a: Place the figure and name the empty field. Example: Vast negative space around [Subject], the figure small, absence as weight, Antonioni emptiness. Say low in frame or far to one side. Forbid extra props in the empty area.

title: One-Point Perspective
narrative: Destiny has a vanishing point when the architecture agrees. Walk toward it and the world funnels.
Stand in the middle and the world presents. A small step off axis becomes a scandal because the construction was so true.

It is the wrong tool in a room with no parallel receding edges, or when the scene should feel found rather than designed. Forcing a tunnel onto a forest is a lie unless the trees were planted as a nave.
Centering a face is not enough. If the walls do not recede to one point, you have central framing in a box.
how: Align the lens with the centerline of the architecture. Keep verticals vertical (shift, a level, or a longer lens farther back).
Place the vanishing point on a face, on a door, or on empty infinity. A moderate wide (24mm to 35mm) shows the funnel.
Too wide bows the walls. Prompt: One-point perspective corridor toward [Subject] or through them, vanishing point on axis, Kubrick infinity.
when: Use it for hotels, spaceships, naves, bunkers, and any fate that should feel designed. Do not square up a messy street and call it one-point because a face is in the middle.
vs: Leading Lines may converge without a full axial construction. Centered Composition plants the subject on the axis but may be a flat altar with no tunnel.
Vanishing Point is the meeting place itself and can sit off-axis in two-point perspective. Symmetry often arrives with one-point, but a tunnel can hide an unmatched object as the break.
Architexture may flatten facade as texture instead of aiming it.
examples_film: The Shining aims Overlook corridors at a point that feels like destiny. 2001: A Space Odyssey uses axial interiors as designed future.
Leon and The Grand Budapest Hotel also square halls and lobbies so order is the air you breathe. Grammar of construction, not a carpet to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a centered portrait in a hall shot from a corner. The tell is two vanishing points, a wall receding on one side only.
The fix is to move onto the axis until left and right converge together, or to own Vanishing Point as a two-point street.

faq.q: What is one-point perspective in film?
faq.a: The camera is square to a plane. Parallel receding lines meet at one vanishing point, often on the central axis. Halls, naves, and designed interiors become tunnels or ceremonies.

faq.q: One-Point Perspective vs Centered Composition
faq.a: Centered composition puts the subject on the axis. One-point perspective constructs space toward a single vanishing point. You can center a face against a flat wall with no tunnel. You can also shoot a one-point hall with the actor off to the side as a break.

faq.q: When should I use one-point perspective?
faq.a: Use it when architecture can funnel: hotels, ships, churches, bunkers, a fate that feels designed. Do not fake it in irregular space, and do not confuse a centered head with a vanishing construction.

faq.q: How do I prompt one-point perspective for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for one vanishing point on axis and a square camera. Example: One-point perspective corridor toward [Subject] or through them, vanishing point on axis, Kubrick infinity. Name the corridor. Add verticals true.

title: Reflections
narrative: Show looking and the looked-at together and you skip a cut. A man and a woman speak through a booth.
A face and a street stack in a shop window. Identity splits without a dissolve.

It is the wrong tool when the reflection is an unreadable smear, or when it cheats physics (a mirror that does not answer a head turn). If you cannot map the sightline, the audience will feel the fake even if they cannot name it.
Reflections can dirty a frame or frame-in-frame a second world. Decide which space is brighter.
The brighter side writes itself onto the darker glass.
how: Map optics before you light. Control which side is hotter: the reflection needs a brighter source to read on glass.
Hide the camera, or let it appear if that is the joke. Keep gaze and reflection geometrically honest.
Polarizers kill or manage bounce. Water needs an angle and a still or living surface.
Prompt: Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane.
when: Use it for split identity, conversations that cannot be face to face, cities on windows, a child seeing a parent in a cabinet. Do not add a random mirror because the set has one.
vs: Frame within Frame uses a hard inner rectangle. A reflection may be a smear, a stack, or a perfect copy.
Silhouette can appear in glass as outline. Screen in Screen is an electronic or projected picture, not a bounce.
Dirty Frame often uses glass as an edge chew. Here the glass is the sentence.
Windows may include reflections, but windows as a technique are stacked apertures of lives.
examples_film: The Lady from Shanghai multiplies positions in a mirror maze until aiming becomes impossible. Paris, Texas stages Travis and Jane across a one-way-glass booth so seeing is not symmetrical.
In the Mood for Love catches bodies in glass and rain. Contact uses a cabinet mirror in a child's race down a hall: reflection as geography.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a pasted-on double, or a mirror that ignores head movement. The tell is a reflection that does not match angle, brightness, or motion.
The fix is to build a real optic: brighter observed side, correct eyeline, and a surface that could actually see both.

faq.q: What is reflections in film?
faq.a: Glass, water, chrome, or a mirror puts two spaces into one picture. Observer and observed can share a plane. The bounce must obey optics: angle, brightness, and motion.

faq.q: Reflections vs Frame within Frame
faq.a: A frame within a frame is a second rectangle, often a door or window opening. A reflection is an optical copy or overlay on a surface. A window can do both: it can be an aperture and a mirror at once if you light both sides.

faq.q: When should I use reflections?
faq.a: Use them to show looking and the looked-at together, to split a self, or to have a conversation that cannot be face to face. Do not insert a mirror as furniture with no optical job.

faq.q: How do I prompt reflections for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the surface and both parties. Example: Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane. Specify one-way glass, shop window, or water. For video, demand the reflection match head movement.

title: Repetition and Pattern
narrative: Systems, armies, hotels, and factories love this diagram. Who owns space is the grid.
A person is a unit until they fail to match. That failure (an empty desk, a red coat, a late soldier) becomes the subject without a closer lens.
It is the wrong tool when the location is unique and irregular. Forcing a pattern onto a messy apartment is a graphic lie unless the character is trying to impose one.
Pattern can also return in time: the same blocking on a different day. That is structural echo.
Compositionally it still needs a recognizable spatial rhyme so the audience can measure change.
how: Find a repeating unit and put the camera where the unit tiles: elevation of a facade, a long lens compressing a row, an overhead of desks. Align so the repeat is countable.

Place the break on a power position (a missing unit, a different color, a still figure in a marching line). Prompt: Repeating pattern around [Subject], columns, windows, soldiers, a break in the pattern as the story.
when: Use it for institutions and copies: hotels, offices, armies, data centers, choruses. Do not use it as wallpaper if nothing can break.
vs: Symmetry is a mirror, which is one kind of repeat. Pattern can run in a line or a field without mirroring.
Bird's-Eye View often reveals pattern by removing horizon. Architexture treats material and facade as texture until the person is a detail.
Pattern is the countable grid inside that texture. One-Point Perspective can aim the repeat into a tunnel.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel tiles uniforms, doors, and pastry boxes so a scuff reads. The Matrix uses copies as a philosophical pattern.

Shaun of the Dead rhymes a trip to the shop across a changed world. Jaws and The Empire Strikes Back also teach recurrence in sound, a cousin of visual echo: a figure that returns until it is a system.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is busy production design. The tell is lots of stuff and no countable unit.
The fix is to pick one motif, align the camera to tile it, and isolate the one mismatch.

faq.q: What is repetition and pattern in film?
faq.a: Shapes, colors, lines, positions, or actions repeat until the frame reads as a system. The pattern sets expectation. A break in the pattern is often the subject. Formal rhyme can also return on another day.

faq.q: Repetition and Pattern vs Symmetry
faq.a: Symmetry mirrors across an axis. Pattern repeats a unit in a row, a grid, or in time. A line of hotel doors can be a pattern without left matching right. A mirrored lobby can be symmetrical with only two wings.

faq.q: When should I use repetition and pattern?
faq.a: Use it for systems: armies, hotels, factories, offices, choruses. Use a break when someone fails to be a unit. Skip it in irregular private space unless the character is imposing order.

faq.q: How do I prompt repetition and pattern for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the repeating unit and the exception. Example: Repeating pattern around [Subject], columns, windows, soldiers, a break in the pattern as the story. Count the units if you can. Specify the break.

title: Rule of Thirds
narrative: Treat the frame as a diagram of who owns space. Thirds is a default, not a law.
A face on a power intersection hands the bigger rectangle to the look, the weather, or the threat. The strip behind the head is leftover, not decoration.
It is the wrong tool when the beat needs a formal altar, a trap, or a joke about order. Dead-center ritual, short-sided panic, and poster symmetry all break the grid on purpose.
If you apply thirds to every close-up, the diagram stops meaning anything. A model that hears only balanced composition will center the face and split the sky in half.
Name which intersection holds the eyes and which third holds the horizon.
how: Turn on the 3x3 overlay on the monitor. Place eyes, a head, or a landmark on an intersection, not in the dead middle of a cell.
Keep the camera level unless a roll is the point. A 35mm to 50mm keeps the grid honest.
Ultra-wide glass stretches the outer thirds into cartoon corners. Telephoto compresses them into stacked bands.
Prompt: Rule-of-thirds placement of [Subject] on a power intersection, horizon on a third, breathing room in the look direction.
when: Use it on a landscape walk, a single looking off, or an establishing wide that must feel occupied without becoming an altar. Do not treat it as a religion on every close-up, title card, or ritual tableau.
vs: 618 instead of one-third. Lead Room is the horizontal air that thirds usually create for a look or a walk.
Centered Composition refuses the offset and puts the subject on the axis. Short Siding is the opposite diagram: the look is crushed against the edge it faces.
examples_film: Classical coverage treats thirds as the default diagram for singles and landscapes. Lawrence of Arabia parks horizons on a third so desert owns the rest of the frame.
Days of Heaven does the same with prairie and sky. There Will Be Blood often offsets a figure so land outweighs the person.
These are grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is dead-center portrait posing as thirds. The tell is a face on the optical axis with equal sky and equal leftover on both ears.
The fix is to slide the eyes to an intersection and give the look the larger field, or admit you wanted Central Framing and shoot that instead.

faq.q: What is rule of thirds in film?
faq.a: It is a 3x3 grid overlaid on the frame. Important masses sit on the lines or at the four intersections so the picture is offset by default. The larger remaining field usually belongs to the look, the land, or the threat.

faq.q: Rule of Thirds vs Golden Ratio
faq.a: Thirds splits at 33 percent. A golden-ratio or phi grid splits nearer 38 and 62 percent, a slightly tighter offset, sometimes described as a spiral. Both refuse dead center. Thirds is the faster default on a set. Phi is a quieter proportional claim.

faq.q: When should I use rule of thirds?
faq.a: Use it when a figure or horizon should share the frame with a larger field they do not occupy. A walk, a look off, a landscape single. Skip it when the scene is a ritual, a trap, or a poster that needs the axis.

faq.q: How do I prompt rule of thirds for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the intersection and the horizon line. Example: Rule-of-thirds placement of [Subject] on a power intersection, horizon on a third, breathing room in the look direction. Say left or right. If you only write balanced, the model will center the face.
